hook.text: The most famous coffee legend begins with an Ethiopian goatherd named Kaldi—and his mysteriously energetic goats.

buildup.text: Kaldi noticed his goats dancing wildly after eating red berries from a certain bush on the highland plateau.

discovery.text: He brought the berries to a monastery. A monk threw them into fire in disgust—and the aroma of roasting coffee filled the air.

twist.text: The story first appears in print in 1671—over a thousand years after coffee was likely first used. It may be entirely invented.

climax.text: Despite its uncertain origin, the Kaldi legend is retold on coffee bags, café walls, and brand stories worldwide.

punchline.text: A goatherd, dancing goats, and an accidental roast. Coffee's founding myth endures.

quiz.question: When did the Kaldi legend first appear in print?
options: 1671 — over a thousand years after coffee was likely first used

topics.title: Shen Nung and the Falling Leaf

hook.text: Chinese legend says Emperor Shen Nung discovered tea in 2737 BCE when a leaf blew into his pot of boiling water.

buildup.text: Shen Nung was known as the 'Divine Farmer'—a mythical emperor who tested hundreds of plants for their medicinal properties.

discovery.text: He tasted the infused water and found it refreshing and clarifying. This, the legend says, was the birth of tea.

twist.text: Shen Nung is mythological—no evidence he existed. But the story anchors tea's identity as a natural, accidental discovery.

climax.text: The falling-leaf myth is central to Chinese tea culture. It frames tea as a gift from nature, not human invention.

punchline.text: A breeze, a leaf, a curious emperor. Tea's origin story is pure poetry.

quiz.question: According to legend, how did Shen Nung discover tea?
options: A tea leaf blew into his pot of boiling water
He bought it from a merchant

topics.title: Omar the Dervish: Coffee from Exile

hook.text: A Yemeni legend says a Sufi mystic named Omar discovered coffee while starving in exile outside the city of Mocha.

buildup.text: Banished from Mocha, Omar found bright red berries in the wilderness. He boiled them to make a bitter, sustaining drink.

discovery.text: The drink kept him alive and alert for days. When word reached Mocha, the city recalled him as a healer and saint.

twist.text: The port city of Mocha later became synonymous with coffee. The word 'mocha' traces directly to this ancient Yemeni port.

climax.text: Omar's legend ties coffee to Sufi spirituality—a drink that aids prayer, meditation, and marathon devotional practice.

punchline.text: Exile, hunger, red berries, and survival. Coffee's Yemeni origin is a saint's story.

quiz.question: What city is connected to Omar's coffee legend and later became synonymous with coffee?

hook.text: A Buddhist legend says tea grew from the severed eyelids of Bodhidharma, the monk who brought Zen to China.

buildup.text: Bodhidharma vowed to meditate for nine years without sleeping. When his eyelids drooped, he cut them off in frustration.

discovery.text: Where his eyelids fell, tea bushes sprouted. The leaves carried his determination—keeping all who drink them awake.

twist.text: This legend is more popular in Japan than China. It connects tea directly to Zen discipline and spiritual endurance.

climax.text: The eyelid myth explains why tea and Zen monasteries are inseparable in East Asian culture. Tea sustains meditation.

punchline.text: Severed eyelids, sprouting bushes, endless wakefulness. Tea's darkest origin story.

quiz.question: According to the legend, why does tea keep people awake?
options: It came from a magical spring
It grew from Bodhidharma's severed eyelids, carrying his determination

topics.title: The Oromo Warriors and Coffee Balls

hook.text: Before coffee was brewed as a drink, Ethiopia's Oromo warriors ate it—ground into balls with animal fat for energy.

buildup.text: These coffee-fat balls were portable, calorie-dense, and provided a caffeine boost for long marches and battles.

discovery.text: This is likely coffee's true earliest use—not as a drink, but as a food. The brewing came centuries later.

twist.text: Modern energy bars and caffeine gels echo this ancient practice. The Oromo were the original biohackers.

climax.text: The Oromo never received credit in most coffee histories. Colonial writers preferred Kaldi's myth over African truth.

punchline.text: Not a drink—a weapon fuel. Coffee was eaten before it was ever sipped.

quiz.question: How did Oromo warriors originally consume coffee?
options: Ground into balls with animal fat for portable energy

topics.title: Lu Yu: The Sage of Tea

hook.text: Lu Yu wrote 'The Classic of Tea' around 760 CE—the world's first book entirely about tea. It transformed tea from drink to art.

buildup.text: Orphaned as a child and raised in a Buddhist monastery, Lu Yu spent decades studying tea cultivation and preparation.

discovery.text: His book covered water quality, utensils, leaf grades, correct boiling, and even the spiritual state of the brewer.

twist.text: After his death, Lu Yu was deified. Tea merchants placed his statue in their shops—pouring tea over it for luck.

climax.text: Lu Yu's work codified tea culture for 1,200+ years. Chinese, Japanese, and Korean tea traditions all reference his text.

punchline.text: One orphan, one book, twelve centuries of influence. Lu Yu made tea sacred.

quiz.question: What did Lu Yu write?
options: 'The Classic of Tea' — the first book entirely about tea, around 760 CE

hook.text: In the 1600s, a Sufi pilgrim named Baba Budan smuggled seven coffee beans out of Yemen—strapped to his belly.

buildup.text: Yemen jealously guarded its coffee monopoly. Exporting fertile beans was forbidden; only roasted (dead) seeds could leave.

discovery.text: Baba Budan planted his seven beans in the hills of southern India. They thrived. India became a coffee-growing nation.

twist.text: The hills where he planted are still called 'Baba Budan Giri' today. They remain one of India's premier coffee regions.

climax.text: His seven beans ended Yemen's monopoly. Every coffee plant outside Arabia and Ethiopia may trace to similar smuggling.

punchline.text: Seven beans, one belly, a broken monopoly. Coffee's spread was an act of holy theft.

quiz.question: Why did Baba Budan have to smuggle coffee beans out of Yemen?
options: Yemen forbade exporting fertile beans to protect its monopoly

topics.title: Catherine of Braganza: Tea's Royal Ambassador

hook.text: When Portuguese princess Catherine married England's Charles II in 1662, she brought her tea-drinking habit to the British court.

buildup.text: Tea was barely known in England at the time. Catherine made it fashionable among aristocrats by serving it daily at court.

discovery.text: The English upper class copied the queen. Tea transitioned from exotic curiosity to essential social ritual within a generation.

twist.text: Catherine's dowry included the port of Bombay—later the hub of British trade with tea-producing regions of Asia.

climax.text: One woman's personal preference reshaped an entire nation's culture. Britain became the world's greatest tea-drinking nation.

punchline.text: A Portuguese queen, an English court, and a daily cup. A nation was converted.

quiz.question: How did Catherine of Braganza influence British tea culture?
options: She brought her tea-drinking habit to court, making it fashionable among aristocrats

hook.text: In 1848, Scottish botanist Robert Fortune disguised himself as a Chinese merchant and stole China's tea secrets for Britain.

buildup.text: The British East India Company hired Fortune to smuggle tea plants and manufacturing knowledge out of China's interior.

discovery.text: Fortune learned that black and green tea come from the same plant—a secret China had kept for centuries. Processing, not variety.

twist.text: He shipped 20,000 tea plants and expert Chinese tea makers to India. Britain built its tea empires on this theft.

climax.text: Fortune's espionage ended China's tea monopoly and shifted global power. India surpassed China as the world's top tea exporter.

punchline.text: Disguise, deception, 20,000 plants. The biggest heist in beverage history.

quiz.question: What crucial tea secret did Robert Fortune discover in China?
options: Black and green tea come from the same plant—processing makes the difference

topics.title: Alfred Peet: Godfather of American Specialty Coffee

hook.text: Dutch immigrant Alfred Peet opened Peet's Coffee in Berkeley, California in 1966—and changed how Americans tasted coffee.

buildup.text: Peet grew up in his father's coffee trade in the Netherlands. He was appalled by the weak, stale coffee Americans drank.

discovery.text: Peet roasted small batches of high-quality beans dark and fresh. Customers tasted the difference immediately—it was a revelation.

twist.text: Three early customers—Baldwin, Siegl, and Bowker—founded Starbucks in 1971 using Peet's roasting methods.

climax.text: Without Peet, there's no Starbucks, no specialty movement, no third wave. He lit the match; America's coffee revolution followed.

punchline.text: One immigrant, one small shop, one higher standard. American coffee was reborn.

quiz.question: How did Alfred Peet influence Starbucks?
options: Three of his customers founded Starbucks using his methods and standards

hook.text: On December 16, 1773, American colonists dumped 342 chests of British tea into Boston Harbor—igniting a revolution.

buildup.text: Britain taxed tea without colonial representation. The tax wasn't huge, but the principle of control enraged colonists.

discovery.text: Disguised as Mohawk Indians, about 100 men boarded three ships and destroyed 46 tons of tea worth £10,000 (millions today).

twist.text: After the protest, drinking tea became unpatriotic. Americans switched to coffee—a shift that persists 250 years later.

climax.text: The Boston Tea Party was the spark for the American Revolution. A beverage tax helped create a nation.

punchline.text: 342 chests of tea, one harbor, a new nation. Coffee became America's patriotic drink.

quiz.question: How did the Boston Tea Party affect American beverage culture?
options: Drinking tea became unpatriotic — Americans switched to coffee

topics.title: The Opium Wars: Tea's Deadly Trade

hook.text: Britain's tea addiction created a huge trade deficit with China. The solution? Flood China with opium to balance the books.

buildup.text: By the 1830s, Britain imported millions of pounds of Chinese tea but had little that China wanted to buy in return.

discovery.text: Britain grew opium in India and smuggled it into China—creating millions of addicts and reversing the trade deficit.

twist.text: When China tried to stop the opium trade, Britain declared war. Two Opium Wars forced China to accept the drug trade.

climax.text: Tea's demand fueled one of history's most devastating drug crises. The cup of tea in London had a dark trail back to China.

punchline.text: A cup of tea, a trail of opium, two wars. Demand has consequences.

quiz.question: Why did Britain sell opium to China?
options: To balance a trade deficit caused by massive tea imports from China

hook.text: Before coffee, Europe's daily drink was beer—even at breakfast. Coffee replaced alcohol-fueled thinking with sober debate.

buildup.text: Coffeehouses became 'penny universities' in 17th-century London—pay a penny for coffee and join intellectual conversation.

discovery.text: The French and American revolutions were planned in coffeehouses. Voltaire drank 50 cups a day. Diderot wrote in cafés.

twist.text: Steven Johnson argues coffee drove the Enlightenment—swapping a depressant for a stimulant changed how people thought.

climax.text: Science, finance, journalism, and democracy all advanced in spaces fueled by coffee. The Age of Reason was caffeinated.

punchline.text: From beer to coffee, from foggy to sharp. A beverage switch changed civilization.

quiz.question: Why do some historians link coffee to the Enlightenment?
options: It replaced alcohol as the daily drink, enabling sober intellectual debate

topics.title: Napoleon's Continental Blockade and Chicory Coffee

hook.text: When Napoleon blockaded European ports in 1806, coffee imports stopped. France and Germany desperately sought substitutes.

buildup.text: Real coffee became impossibly expensive. People tried roasted barley, acorns, and figs as replacements—all terrible.

discovery.text: Chicory root—roasted and ground—became the most successful substitute. It was bitter, dark, and vaguely coffee-like.

twist.text: New Orleans still blends chicory with coffee today. The tradition came from French colonists who survived Napoleon's blockade.

climax.text: The blockade proved coffee's hold on Europe. People chose fake substitutes over abandoning the ritual.

punchline.text: No ships, no beans, roasted roots instead. War couldn't kill the coffee habit.

quiz.question: Why does New Orleans still use chicory in its coffee?
options: The tradition came from French colonists who used it during Napoleon's blockade

hook.text: Brazil's coffee empire began with a seduction scheme. In 1727, a Portuguese officer smuggled seeds out of French Guiana.

buildup.text: France guarded its Guianan coffee plantations fiercely. No viable seeds or plants could legally leave the colony.

discovery.text: Lieutenant Francisco de Melo Palheta was sent to settle a border dispute—and secretly to obtain coffee plants by any means.

twist.text: Palheta charmed the French governor's wife. At his farewell banquet, she gave him a bouquet hiding coffee seedlings inside.

climax.text: Those seedlings founded Brazil's coffee industry. By 1850, Brazil produced more coffee than the rest of the world combined.

punchline.text: A bouquet, hidden seedlings, a global empire. Brazil's coffee began with romance.

quiz.question: How did Brazil originally obtain coffee plants?
options: A Portuguese officer smuggled seedlings hidden in a bouquet from French Guiana

hook.text: In 1511, the governor of Mecca banned coffee—claiming it was an intoxicant that violated Islamic law.

buildup.text: Khair Bey gathered scholars and physicians who testified that coffee was harmful to body and mind. Coffeehouses were shut down.

discovery.text: The real reason was political. Coffeehouses were where dissenters gathered, talked freely, and criticized authorities.

twist.text: The Ottoman Sultan overruled the ban within weeks. He loved coffee and pointed out that the Quran never mentioned it.

climax.text: Khair Bey was later executed—for corruption, not the ban. But the episode proved coffee's power to frighten rulers.

punchline.text: Banned, overruled, the governor executed. Coffee won its first political battle.

quiz.question: Why did the governor of Mecca really ban coffee in 1511?
options: Coffeehouses were gathering places for political dissent and free speech

hook.text: In 1674, London women published 'The Women's Petition Against Coffee,' complaining their husbands spent all day in coffeehouses.

buildup.text: The petition claimed coffee made men impotent, lazy, and absent from home. Wives were fed up with empty beds and cold dinners.

discovery.text: Men responded with 'The Men's Answer'—arguing that coffee improved their stamina and intellect, making them better husbands.

twist.text: The petitions were likely satirical—18th-century social commentary disguised as a gender battle. But the social tension was real.

climax.text: Charles II tried banning coffeehouses in 1675. The ban lasted just 11 days before public outcry reversed it.

punchline.text: Women protested, the king banned, the people revolted. Coffee was unstoppable.

quiz.question: How long did King Charles II's 1675 coffeehouse ban last?
options: Just 11 days before public outcry reversed it

hook.text: Prussia's Frederick the Great tried to ban common people from drinking coffee in 1777—insisting they drink beer instead.

buildup.text: Frederick argued that coffee drained money from the Prussian economy. He feared rising imports would bankrupt the state.

discovery.text: He created 'coffee sniffers'—government agents who roamed streets, sniffing for the aroma of illegal home coffee roasting.

twist.text: The policy was wildly unpopular and impossible to enforce. Citizens roasted in secret, like prohibition later.

climax.text: Frederick himself was a notorious coffee lover. He drank it daily—brewed with champagne instead of water, by some accounts.

punchline.text: A king who banned coffee but drank it himself. Hypocrisy brewed perfectly.

quiz.question: What were 'coffee sniffers' in Frederick the Great's Prussia?
options: Government agents who sniffed for illegal home coffee roasting

hook.text: In the 1750s, Sweden's King Gustav III tried to prove coffee was poison—using an experiment on condemned prisoners.

buildup.text: Two identical twins were sentenced to death. One was ordered to drink three pots of coffee daily, the other three pots of tea.

discovery.text: The experiment was monitored by physicians for years. Both prisoners survived long beyond expectations—outliving their doctors.

twist.text: The tea drinker died first—at age 83. The coffee drinker lived even longer. Coffee was vindicated, and the ban was dropped.

climax.text: King Gustav III was assassinated in 1792—long before the experiment concluded. He never saw coffee's acquittal.

punchline.text: The king died. The doctors died. The coffee drinker lived longest. Case closed.

quiz.question: What happened in the Swedish coffee experiment with twin prisoners?
options: Both lived past 80—the tea drinker died first, vindicating coffee

hook.text: When coffee reached Europe, Catholic advisors asked Pope Clement VIII to ban it—calling it 'Satan's drink' from the Islamic world.

buildup.text: The pope was presented with a cup for judgment around 1600. Catholics feared that coffee's origin in Muslim lands made it unholy.

discovery.text: The pope tasted it and declared: 'This devil's drink is so delicious we should cheat the devil and baptize it.'

twist.text: This story may be apocryphal—no reliable contemporary source confirms it. But it captures a real cultural moment of acceptance.

climax.text: After the pope's supposed blessing, coffee spread rapidly through Catholic Europe. Venice, Rome, and Vienna embraced it.

punchline.text: Satan's drink, blessed by the pope. One sip overruled centuries of suspicion.

quiz.question: What did Pope Clement VIII supposedly say about coffee?
options: 'This Satan's drink is so delicious we should cheat the devil and baptize it'

hook.text: Espresso was invented because Italians hated waiting. In 1884, Angelo Moriondo patented a machine to brew coffee in seconds.

buildup.text: Traditional brewing took 5+ minutes. Moriondo's steam machine forced water through grounds at pressure, slashing time.

discovery.text: The word 'espresso' means 'pressed out' or 'express'—both referencing the pressure and the speed of delivery.

twist.text: Moriondo never commercialized his machine widely. Gaggia's 1948 lever machine created the espresso we know today.

climax.text: Gaggia's machine produced 9 bars of pressure—enough to create crema, the golden foam that defines modern espresso.

punchline.text: High pressure, golden crema, thirty seconds. Impatience invented espresso.

quiz.question: What does the word 'espresso' literally mean?
options: 'Pressed out' or 'express'—referring to pressure and speed

topics.title: Irish Coffee: A Foggy Night in Foynes

hook.text: Irish coffee was invented in 1943 at a windswept airport in Foynes, Ireland—to warm shivering transatlantic passengers.

buildup.text: Chef Joe Sheridan added whiskey to hot coffee, topped with cream, for passengers whose flight turned back in bad weather.

discovery.text: When a passenger asked 'Is this Brazilian coffee?' Sheridan replied: 'No, it's Irish coffee.' The name stuck forever.

twist.text: Journalist Stanton Delaplane brought the recipe to San Francisco's Buena Vista Café in 1952. It became iconic.

climax.text: The Buena Vista still serves 2,000 Irish coffees daily—the most of any single bar in the world. Sheridan's creation endures.

punchline.text: Bad weather, warm whiskey, floating cream. One stormy night created a global classic.

quiz.question: Where was Irish coffee invented?
options: Foynes airport, Ireland — to warm shivering transatlantic passengers in 1943

topics.title: Chai: India's National Drink Wasn't Always Popular

hook.text: India is the world's biggest tea-drinking nation—but most Indians barely drank tea before the 1900s.

buildup.text: The British grew tea in India for export. Domestic consumption was tiny. Indians preferred water, milk, and local beverages.

discovery.text: The Indian Tea Association launched aggressive marketing in the 1900s—free samples at train stations and factories.

twist.text: Indians rejected plain British-style tea. They added milk, sugar, and spices—creating masala chai, a completely reinvented drink.

climax.text: By independence in 1947, chai was India's national drink. An imported colonial commodity had been domesticated and remade.

punchline.text: Britain pushed tea on India. India turned it into something entirely its own.

quiz.question: How did Indians change British-style tea into masala chai?
options: They added milk, sugar, and spices—completely reinventing the drink

hook.text: Bubble tea was invented in Taiwan in the 1980s when someone added tapioca pearls to iced milk tea—and created a global craze.

buildup.text: Two Taiwanese tea shops both claim the invention. Chun Shui Tang and Hanlin Tea Room have disputed credit for decades.

discovery.text: The chewy tapioca pearls (called 'boba') transformed tea from a simple drink into an interactive, textural experience.

twist.text: A Taiwanese court ruled in 2019 that bubble tea cannot be patented—it's too simple. No one owns the invention.

climax.text: Bubble tea is now a multi-billion dollar global industry. From Taipei to London, boba shops outnumber many traditional cafés.

punchline.text: Tapioca in tea—simple, addictive, unstoppable. A snack-drink conquered the world.

quiz.question: Where was bubble tea invented?
options: Taiwan in the 1980s when tapioca pearls were added to iced milk tea

topics.title: Turkish Coffee: Sand, Cezve, and Fortune

hook.text: Turkish coffee is brewed by boiling ultra-fine grounds in a small brass pot called a cezve—sometimes nestled in hot sand.

buildup.text: The grounds are never filtered. They settle to the bottom of tiny cups, creating a thick, sludgy bed of sediment.

discovery.text: That sediment is used for tasseography—fortune telling. The cup is inverted and patterns are read for the future.

twist.text: UNESCO added Turkish coffee to its Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2013. It's a world civilization.

climax.text: A Turkish proverb says: 'A cup of coffee commits one to 40 years of friendship.' Coffee is a social contract, not just a beverage.

punchline.text: Sand-brewed, unfiltered, fortune in the mud. Turkish coffee is pure ritual.

quiz.question: What is tasseography in Turkish coffee culture?
options: Fortune telling by reading patterns in the coffee sediment left in the cup

hook.text: Most people believe dark roast is 'stronger'—more caffeine, more intensity. The truth is the opposite.

buildup.text: Dark roast beans are larger (expanded by heat) and lighter (moisture lost). Per scoop, you get fewer beans than light roast.

discovery.text: Caffeine is stable through roasting. But dark roast beans weigh less, so a scoop of dark has slightly less caffeine.

twist.text: What people perceive as 'strength' is actually bitter, smoky roast flavor—not caffeine content. Bold taste ≠ high caffeine.

climax.text: If measured by weight (grams), dark and light are nearly identical in caffeine. The myth comes from measuring by volume.

punchline.text: Dark roast tastes bold but isn't stronger. Flavor intensity fooled everyone.

quiz.question: Why does a scoop of dark roast have slightly less caffeine than light?
options: Dark beans are larger and lighter — fewer beans per scoop means less total caffeine

topics.title: Kopi Luwak: The World's Most Controversial Coffee

hook.text: Kopi Luwak is coffee made from beans eaten and excreted by civet cats. It sells for $100–600 per pound.

buildup.text: The legend says digestive enzymes in the civet's gut break down proteins, reducing bitterness and creating a uniquely smooth cup.

discovery.text: Specialty tasters consistently rate Kopi Luwak as mediocre—smoothness increases but complexity disappears.

twist.text: Most commercial Kopi Luwak comes from caged civets force-fed coffee cherries. The 'wild-harvested' story is largely marketing.

climax.text: Animal welfare organizations have condemned the industry. The world's most expensive coffee has one of the worst ethical records.

punchline.text: Exotic, expensive, overhyped, and often cruel. Fame doesn't mean quality.

quiz.question: How do specialty professionals rate Kopi Luwak's taste?
options: Consistently mediocre — smooth but lacking complexity

topics.title: Does Tea Have Less Caffeine Than Coffee?

hook.text: People assume tea has less caffeine than coffee. Pound for pound, tea leaves actually contain MORE caffeine than coffee beans.

buildup.text: Dried tea leaves are about 3.5% caffeine by weight. Coffee beans are about 1.5%. Tea wins on concentration.

discovery.text: But you use far less tea per cup (2g) than coffee (10-15g). Less leaf per cup means less caffeine in the final drink.

twist.text: Tea also contains L-theanine, which moderates caffeine's effect. Tea drinkers feel alert but calm—not jittery like coffee.

climax.text: The 'tea has less caffeine' statement is true for the cup—but false for the leaf. Context determines the answer.

punchline.text: More caffeine in the leaf, less in the cup. Brewing ratio changes everything.

quiz.question: Why does a cup of tea have less caffeine than coffee despite tea leaves having more caffeine by weight?
options: Much less tea leaf (2g) is used per cup compared to coffee grounds (10-15g)

hook.text: Instant coffee was first mass-produced in 1910 by George Washington—not the president, but a Belgian-American inventor.

buildup.text: Washington noticed dried coffee residue on his carafe lid. He realized brewed coffee could be dehydrated and reconstituted.

discovery.text: His Red E Coffee launched in 1910. During WWI, soldiers loved it—they called any instant coffee 'a cup of George.'

twist.text: Nestlé's Nescafé (1938) perfected the formula. Brazil's coffee surplus funded the research—too many beans to sell.

climax.text: Today, instant coffee outsells brewed in most of the world. Only in the US and parts of Europe does fresh brewing dominate.

punchline.text: Dried residue on a lid, a wartime staple, a global default. Accidents scale.

quiz.question: What inspired George Washington to create instant coffee?
options: He noticed dried coffee residue on his silver carafe lid could be reconstituted

topics.title: The Third Wave: Coffee as Craft

hook.text: The 'third wave' treats coffee like wine—obsessing over origin, variety, processing, and the individual farmer who grew it.

buildup.text: First wave was commodity (Folgers). Second wave was café culture (Starbucks). Third wave elevates coffee to craft.

discovery.text: Third-wave roasters buy single-origin, traceable lots. They roast light to showcase terroir and score coffees like wine critics.

twist.text: Critics argue third wave is elitist—$7 pour-overs alienate everyday drinkers and ignore the global majority who drink instant.

climax.text: A possible 'fourth wave' focuses on equity—paying farmers fairly while making quality accessible, not just exclusive.

punchline.text: Commodity, culture, craft, equity. Each wave remakes what coffee means.

quiz.question: What defines third-wave coffee?
options: Treating coffee as artisanal craft — focusing on origin, variety, and terroir
